name: Demeclocycline
lead: Demeclocycline is a semisynthetic tetracycline antibiotic, sold in the United States as Declomycin and as generic tablets, used for infections caused by susceptible organisms such as rickettsiae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia species. [1][2][13] It also blunts the kidney's response to antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin), which makes the kidneys excrete more free water, and clinicians have used this effect off-label for the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). [1][3][13]

The wiki lists it under depuffing because of that water-excreting action. The chain people draw is: less ADH signalling in the collecting duct, more dilute urine, less retained fluid, and so potentially less facial and body puffiness. [1] No published study has tested demeclocycline for facial puffiness or any appearance purpose, and the chain remains a proposed one.

The idea behind interest in demeclocycline for looks is fluid balance. A puffy face is often attributed to retained water, and demeclocycline is one of few medicines whose recognised kidney effect is to make the body excrete more free water; people who discuss it in a depuffing context are drawing on that effect, which in clinical practice is used in people whose blood sodium is abnormally low rather than in people with normal sodium.[13][16]

As with other tetracyclines, its label warns of fetal harm in pregnancy and permanent tooth discoloration if used during tooth development in childhood. Photosensitivity is a well-known feature of this particular tetracycline. [2][6][14]
infobox: Declomycin (also Declostatin, Ledermycin and others abroad)

paras: The label indicates demeclocycline for rickettsial infections such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhus, respiratory infections from Mycoplasma pneumoniae, lymphogranuloma venereum, psittacosis, trachoma and other infections confirmed or suspected to involve susceptible organisms. [2] Wikipedia notes that rising resistance means it is now rarely used for infections. [13] A 1987 review of tetracyclines noted the class remains the agent of choice for Chlamydiae, Rickettsiae, Brucella and Borrelia. [4]

In SIADH, excess ADH leads to water retention and low blood sodium (hyponatraemia). [5] Demeclocycline is not a labelled treatment for it, but its first reported use there dates to 1975 according to Wikipedia, and a 1978 New England Journal of Medicine study reported it to be superior to lithium in chronic SIADH. [3][13] The 1987 review described it as often an agent of choice for this use. [4] Newer vasopressin-receptor antagonists such as tolvaptan may now have superseded it in some settings. [13]

In the encyclopedia account of SIADH, excess ADH makes the kidneys hold on to free water, which dilutes blood sodium and causes cells to swell; mild cases are managed first with fluid restriction and a cause is sought, and demeclocycline is listed for chronic cases when fluid restriction is hard to maintain, with a delay of two to three days before it takes effect and side effects including photosensitivity and kidney toxicity.[16] Alternatives include tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, oral urea and, in some settings, conivaptan.[16] The same account describes cerebral oedema as the swelling concern in SIADH and does not link the condition to facial puffiness.[16]
As an antibiotic, demeclocycline binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA and halting protein synthesis; the effect is bacteriostatic. [1][13]

In the kidney, it reduces the collecting duct's response to ADH. Grokipedia says it may do this by reducing ADH-induced cAMP and aquaporin-2 water channels, increasing free-water excretion without major electrolyte loss; Wikipedia says the exact mechanism is not fully understood and that it acts after ADH binds the V2 receptor. [1][13] It produces a state resembling nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. [13] Aquaporins are also studied more broadly in the context of edema. [11]

Wikipedia describes the kidney effect as interference with adenylyl cyclase activation after ADH binds the V2 receptor, a state that resembles nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and adds that the drug may have psychotropic effects resembling lithium; the exact mechanism is described as not fully understood.[13]

Tetracyclines of the older group, including demeclocycline, are characterised by poor absorption after food, unlike doxycycline and minocycline. [12] Oral bioavailability is reported at 60 to 80 percent, with an elimination half-life of about 10 to 17 hours; it is excreted largely by the kidneys. [1][13] The drug chelates calcium, iron and magnesium, so dairy and antacids reduce absorption. [13]

Demeclocycline, also called demethylchlortetracycline, is derived from a mutant strain of the soil bacterium Streptomyces aureofaciens, and the same species gives its parent compound chlortetracycline.[13] Its use in SIADH was first reported in 1975, and a larger 1978 study found it more effective and better tolerated than lithium carbonate, which was then the only available treatment.[13][3] The drug has been sold as Declomycin, Declostatin, Ledermycin and under several other names in different countries, and it is generally prescription-only.[13]

Wikipedia notes it was officially indicated for bacterial infections and has been used for Lyme disease, acne and bronchitis, with resistance now limiting its use as an antibiotic; vasopressin receptor antagonists may supersede it for SIADH.[13] Wikipedia also states that, like other tetracyclines, it is contraindicated in children and in pregnant or nursing women because it can discolour teeth and affect bone development, and that it binds calcium, iron and magnesium, so dairy products and antacids reduce its absorption.[13]

The label lists gastrointestinal effects such as anorexia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, increased liver enzymes, rare hepatotoxicity and oesophageal ulceration, and class warnings that tetracyclines can cause fetal harm and permanent yellow-grey-brown tooth discoloration if used during tooth development (last half of pregnancy, infancy and childhood to age 8). [2]

Demeclocycline is notable for phototoxicity. A 1971 JAMA controlled trial compared it with methacycline in relation to sunlight, and a 1976 acne study contrasted minocycline's lack of phototoxicity with that seen with demeclocycline. [6][14] A 2019 review describes tetracyclines, demeclocycline and doxycycline among them, as light-activated antibiotics in lab work, reflecting this photochemical reactivity. [15] Grokipedia adds rare pseudotumor cerebri and superinfection. [1] Because of its effect on water handling, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is a recognised consequence. [13]

Sun sensitivity is the effect most relevant to appearance: skin reactions to sunlight are described as typical of this tetracycline, and the 1971 and 1976 studies compared it with other tetracyclines on that point.[13][6][14] Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, with excess urine output and thirst, is the intended effect in SIADH and a recognised consequence in other settings.[13]
No studies found on demeclocycline for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing.

In SIADH, a 1978 NEJM study reported demeclocycline superior to lithium in chronic SIADH. [3] A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined it for polydipsia-hyponatraemia in chronically psychotic patients (1991). [7] A 2023 randomised phase 2 study in hospitalised patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 included only 20 patients in its modified intention-to-treat population (control, 150 mg and 300 mg daily groups) and reported a significant rise in CD4+ T cells in the 150 mg group. [8] Registered trials have also examined demeclocycline fluorescence for delineating brain tumours during surgery (NCT02740933, phase 1, planned n=40). [9]

card.summary: A tetracycline antibiotic that also makes the kidneys excrete free water; nothing links it to facial puffiness.

quick.overview:
Demeclocycline is a prescription tetracycline antibiotic. Doctors have also used it off-label to treat SIADH, because it blunts the kidney's response to antidiuretic hormone.

It is catalogued under depuffing for that water-excreting effect, but no study has tested it for facial puffiness.
quick.mechanism: As an antibiotic it blocks bacterial protein synthesis; as an aquaretic it reduces the collecting duct's response to vasopressin, increasing free water loss.
quick.risks: The label lists gastrointestinal upset, rare liver toxicity, sun sensitivity, and warns of fetal harm and permanent tooth discoloration in children. Antibiotic use also carries resistance and superinfection concerns. It is prescription-only.

chain: Less retained fluid, which could in principle reduce puffiness
angle.text: Demeclocycline is catalogued for depuffing because it increases free-water excretion by blunting ADH action. This is an extrapolation from its use in hyponatraemia; it has not been studied for facial puffiness.
